rawEventDetails: Speaker Akshay Gadre Affiliation University of Washington Details Event Description Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal resolution, Together, these trends create the foundation for an Internet of Radar Things (IoRT) : a dense population of access points, base stations, vehicles, robots, and mobile devices whose radios can sense while they communicate. Unfortunately, a network of these sensing-capable radios operates largely as n isolated monostatic sensors: each independently occupies spectrum, illuminates an overlapping environment, and retains only the echoes at its own small aperture. These discarded paths contain complementary viewpoints that could extend coverage through occlusions, distinguish physical objects from multipath ghosts, and synthesize apertures far larger than any individual device. This talk presents a unique vision to coordinate these distributed radars coherently to turn this world of radios into one mega-radar. In this talk, we will first present the unique capabilities such a coherent future could enable and how we achieve coherence on commodity off-the-shelf radars to demonstrate these solutions. We specifically show how distributed radars can eliminate ghost artifacts and improve sensing capability, how we can extract material characteristics of objects using this large aperture and how we can use coherence-in-motion to develop free-flowing hand-held imaging solutions for mmWave radars. We further demonstrate how these improvements can directly translate to WiFi and cellular radios. Finally, we end the talk by describing open challenges that still need to be addressed to unleash the true potential of the Internet of Radar Things. Bio: Akshay Gadre is an Assistant Professor at Electrical and Computer Engineering department at the University of Washington. He leads the Networking and Emerging Wireless Technologies (NEWT) Lab at the University of Washington where they explore the upcoming application domains such as satellite IoT, mmWave radars and underwater devices, to apply wireless expertise for improving communication and sensing capability of these devices while preserving the security and privacy of sensor data. Further, the lab explores novel interaction mechanisms for future smart devices such as smart gloves and XR systems using novel force sensing and gaze modalities. His previous research at Carnegie Mellon University operated at the intersection of wireless, mobile and cyber-physical systems with special focus on empowering the low-power Internet-of-Things devices deployed on earth and space. NEWT Lab is also translating these technologies to industry partners including General Motors and IDD Aerospace. His work is published in premier wireless and mobile systems venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, Transactions on Sensor Networks and NSDI. Their lab's work has won two best paper awards, four best demo awards, two best-demo runner up awards at these venues. Both Akshay and his students have received the best PhD Forum presentation award at the CPS-IoT Week. Their work has been recognized with the T-Mobile T-Challenge 2024 Most Engaging Presentation Award for their vision of radio digital twins for consumer applications as well as the AFRL SDR University Challenge Best Demo award for developing a cheap SDR platform for exploring satellite networking. He has been also recognized with the ACM SIGBED-SIGSOFT Frank Anger Memorial Award 2021 for his cross-disciplinary work on IoT networking, cyber-security and software engineering. He was also recognized as a Distinguished TPC Member for his services to ACM SenSys 2026. He received his Bachelor of Technology (Honors) and Master of Technology degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from IIT Madras as well as a Ph.D in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. Sponsor NextG Wireless

title: Scaling Certifiable Safety for Embodied AI: From Fixed Domains toward Open-World Autonomy

content: Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. rawEventDetails: Speaker Duy Phuong Nguyen Details Event Description Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. Analytical methods often rely on reduced-order models, whereas numerical methods can provide stronger guarantees but quickly become intractable. Learning scales to high-dimensional systems, yet typically offers only empirical or probabilistic assurances. This dissertation combines the scalability of learning with the rigor of control-theoretic safety. In the first part, we develop certifiable safety filters for a designed world with a fixed Operational Design Domain (ODD), which specifies the admissible dynamics, environmental conditions, disturbances, and failure modes. Safety synthesis is formulated as solving a zero-sum game between the robot and an adversary representing the admissible disturbances. We develop a provably convergent adversarial actor–critic method to approximate the game solution and synthesize neural safety policies for high-dimensional systems. This framework enables full-order safety-filter synthesis and zero-shot deployment across different high-dimensional robotic systems. The learned safety value function can also serve as a state–action control barrier function, recovering the maximal robust safety envelope while minimally modifying the task policy. We further show that sufficiently permissive filtering does not degrade asymptotic performance, enabling reinforcement learning that reaches state-of-the-art performance faster than imperfectly safe methods, with zero violations under a perfect filter. Finally, we show that goal-conditioned reach-avoid safety filters make interventions preserve the task rather than only avoid failure, and expand rather than restrict what robots can safely do, from quadruped parkour to underactuated industrial cranes. The second part extends safety beyond the designed world, where the ODD can no longer be held fixed. We first introduce dynamic ODDs, which condition safety values and policies on operating limits inferred and updated at runtime, allowing the robot to adapt as physical conditions change. However, this is not enough when the relevant hazards and failure modes were never specified in advance. We therefore develop an open-context architecture in which generative models interpret the scene, revise the relevant ODD, and select control-grounded safety tools through a representation shared with classical autonomy. This progression lays the foundation for extending certifiable safety from fixed physical envelopes toward open, human-centered autonomy. An embargo has been approved for this thesis. To view a copy of the thesis please stop by the EQUAD Graduate office B209. Adviser: Jaime Fernández Fisac

rawEventDetails: Speaker Sarita Adve Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Abstract: Immersive computing, including virtual, augmented, and mixed reality (collectively, extended reality or XR), integrates the virtual with the physical. Immersive systems enable AI to escape from the chatbot on a 2D screen into the 3D world around us, where it can perceive, understand, and act alongside the people who live and work there. AI, in turn, is making immersive systems more capable. We refer to the convergence of immersive computing and AI as immersive intelligence. Immersive intelligence places demands on computer systems that are orders of magnitude beyond what current systems deliver: real-time inference over many interacting models, within the power envelope of all-day wearable devices, with quality ultimately judged by the human experience. Meeting these demands requires distributing immersive intelligence across the wearable, nearby devices, the edge, and the datacenter, and evaluating the resulting designs with new human-centric metrics. I will discuss recent work and what it suggests about the architecture of these systems, from the wearable to the datacenter, and about the opportunities ahead for the architecture and systems community. The talk will draw on ILLIXR, our open-source end-to-end XR system testbed, which supports distributed XR and first-of-their-kind AI-enabled XR capabilities, and on the IMMERSE Center for Immersive Computing at Illinois, which brings together research on immersive technologies, applications, and human experience. Bio: Sarita Adve is the Richard T. Cheng Professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her research interests span the system stack, from hardware to applications, with a current focus on immersive intelligence. She directs the IMMERSE Center for Immersive Computing, which brings together expertise in immersive technologies, applications, and human experience to perform research, educate a new workforce, and build infrastructure to enable a new era of immersive computing. Her group released ILLIXR (Illinois Extended Reality testbed), an open-source end-to-end extended reality (XR) system and research testbed that is used widely. She led the XR section of SRC's MAPT 2.0 roadmap for the semiconductor industry. Her early work on data-race-free memory consistency models and later work on the memory models for the Java and C++ programming languages form the foundation for memory models used in most hardware and software systems today. She is also known for her work on heterogeneous architectures and software-driven hardware resiliency. She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a fellow of the ACM, IEEE, and AAAS. She has received several awards, including the ACM/IEEE-CS Ken Kennedy award, the ACM SIGARCH Maurice Wilkes award, and the ACM SIGARCH Alan D. Berenbaum Distinguished Service award. As ACM SIGARCH chair, she co-founded the CARES movement, winner of the CRA distinguished service award, to address discrimination and harassment in computer science research events. She received her PhD from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and her B.Tech. from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

title: Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design for Programmable Sensor-Fusion Perception and Scalable In-Memory Computing
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. rawEventDetails: Speaker Rakshit Pathak Details Event Description Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. Exploiting both forms of sensing requires fusion algorithms that generalize across modalities and tasks, as well as computing platforms that can execute them with high energy efficiency while retaining programmability. This dissertation addresses these needs through algorithm-hardware co-design, spanning the fusion model, processor architecture, silicon prototypes and system infrastructure. First, a generalized Deep-Learning Sensor-Fusion (DL-SF) model is developed, which projects embedded-sensor features into sparse two-dimensional feature maps via domain transformation, scales them to the receptive field of each layer, and concatenates them throughout a convolutional backbone. Across four bookend applications (depth-map generation, 3D human-pose estimation, human trajectory forecasting and human-activity recognition), the DL-SF model improves accuracy and sample efficiency relative to vision-only, early-fusion and late-fusion baselines, for example requiring 3,680 rather than 16k training samples to reach iso-accuracy (98.2%) in activity recognition. Second, the computational structure of the DL-SF model is analyzed to drive the design of a heterogeneous processor in 28nm CMOS, integrating a RISC-V CPU with ISA extensions for embedded-sensor feature extraction, an NVDLA-based convolution accelerator, a Q22.10 fixed-point domain transformation unit, and a memory-data densifier for dense/sparse activation referencing. The prototype executes all four applications end-to-end with 9.3 to 28.1× lower energy and 300 to 500× lower latency than software execution on the CPU, and 15.6 to 24.6× lower energy than reference GPU implementations. Third, this dissertation develops the host-to-chip system infrastructure for a scalable in-memory-computing (IMC) neural-network accelerator in 16nm CMOS, comprising a 4×4 array of IMC cores connected by an on-chip network. This includes the chip interface connecting off-chip signals through the activation and weight buffers to the on-chip network, a PCIe-based FPGA controller using the RIFFA framework, an FPGA emulator of the IMC core for pre-silicon software validation, and a C library that bridges Python-level neural-network mapping tools to the hardware. This infrastructure enabled the measurement and demonstration of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet networks on the prototype. Adviser: Naveen Verma
summaryRaw: Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design for Programmable Sensor-Fusion Perception and Scalable In-Memory Computing

rawEventDetails: Speaker Kyle Forhna Affiliation Stanford Energy Postdoctoral Fellow, Physics PhD Details Event Description Abstract: Growing electricity demands and climate targets are forcing unprecedented restructuring of our electrical grid. Solving these issues requires increasing renewable energy generation and storage capacity at exponential rates. To achieve this, we must rapidly improve existing technologies while discovering and optimising new materials and devices at unprecedented speed to ensure diverse, secure energy supply with resilient, domestic supply chains. However, unlike incumbent semiconductors, next-generation energy devices are highly disordered on multiple length scales, and this has massive implications for their operating principles, performance and stability. Understanding and improving these devices requires high resolution and throughput characterisation of this multiscale disorder. In this presentation, I will describe the development of multimodal microscopy toolkits sensitive to optoelectronic and electrochemical activity, crystal structure, and chemical composition. I will then detail their application to materials relevant for renewable energy generation and storage. Using halide perovskite semiconductors as a highly disordered model system, I will discuss the origins of their remarkable tolerance to extremely high concentrations of defects, the chemical and structural origins of this disorder, and how this disorder is predictive of solar cell performance and degradation. Then, in a range of rechargeable battery chemistries, I will show, with single particle resolution, how disorder can seed capacity loss and irreversible degradation, but can also unlock exciting new applications. I will highlight disorder as both a unifying challenge and design axis across a range of crucial technologies. Bio: Kyle Frohna is a Stanford Energy Postdoctoral Fellow in the Departments of Materials Science & Engineering and Electrical Engineering working with Professors William Chueh and Daniel Congreve where he develops tools to study batteries under operational conditions. He completed his PhD in Physics and an EPSRC Doctoral Prize Postdoctoral Fellowship at the Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge in the group of Professor Sam Stranks studying halide perovskite materials and solar cells at the nanoscale and received the Woodruff PhD Thesis Prize from the Institute of Physics. He received his B.Sc. in Nanoscience: The Physics and Chemistry of Advanced Materials from Trinity College Dublin, Ireland, close to where he grew up. His research focuses on how to characterise, understand and manipulate disorder to improve next-generation energy materials with a latest thrust on coupling high-throughput experimentation with advanced characterisation. His work has been recognised with awards including the Cambridge Trust Scholarship, Schiff Foundation Studentship, Robert Gardiner Scholarship and the Winton Sustainability Fellowship. Outside of research, he is an avid heavy metal drummer and likes to practice olympic weightlifting. Sponsor Dane de Quilettes Contact Patricia Kuczmarski [email protected]

title: Information Technologies at the Fundamental Physical Limits
content: Abstract Fundamental physical laws set the performance limits of computing, communications, and sensing. Advances in nanotechnology and integrated circuits have brought these technologies closer to their classical limits, while quantum resources offer ways to extend their performance. In this talk, I will discuss the physical and information-theoretic bounds that govern these systems and present large-scale integrated systems in silicon photonics and electronics designed to approach them. rawEventDetails: Speaker Volkan Gurses Affiliation MIT Details Event Description Abstract Fundamental physical laws set the performance limits of computing, communications, and sensing. Advances in nanotechnology and integrated circuits have brought these technologies closer to their classical limits, while quantum resources offer ways to extend their performance. In this talk, I will discuss the physical and information-theoretic bounds that govern these systems and present large-scale integrated systems in silicon photonics and electronics designed to approach them. The talk will cover experimental demonstrations and proposed architectures across three areas: quantum computing on CMOS and hybrid classical–quantum computing; quantum coherent transceivers that encode information in non-classical light, with a path beyond the Shannon limit toward the Holevo limit; and quantum phased arrays and squeezed-light sensors for sensing beyond the standard quantum limit toward the Heisenberg limit. For each system, I will connect the underlying theory to integrated circuit design, experimental results, and applications. I will conclude with a path toward scalable, deployable technologies within today’s CMOS infrastructure. Bio Volkan Gurses is a postdoctoral researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a lecturer at the California Institute of Technology, and a visiting researcher at NVIDIA Research. He received his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering with a subject minor in Physics and his M.S. in Electrical Engineering from the California Institute of Technology, and his B.S. in Electrical Engineering with Research Option from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His research is broadly on integrated systems, with a focus on studying the fundamental physical and information-theoretic limits of technologies (e.g., Landauer, Holevo, Heisenberg) and developing integrated systems that can operate at these limits. During his Ph.D., he founded a chip design startup named Foundation Silicon after winning the Caltech Entrepreneurship Prize. He was additionally awarded the Carver Mead New Adventures Fund, R. David Middlebrook Fellowship, Caltech EAS Division Fellowship, Tau Beta Pi Fellowship, IEEE MTT-S Undergraduate/Pre-Graduate Scholarship, European Union Contest for Young Scientists CERN Special Donated Prize, and First Prize in the Turkish National Research Contest, and he was named a Rising Star by Cell Press. Sponsor Electrical & Computer Engineering

rawEventDetails: Speaker Yuhao Zhu Affiliation University of Rochester Details Event Description Abstract: Computers are increasingly integrated into embodied systems that operate in complex real-world environments, such as autonomous robots and smart wearable/Extended Reality (XR) glasses. These systems must continuously sense and interpret the physical world while also generating information that engages human perceptual and cognitive systems. This talk argues that programming and architecting future computer systems must integrate sensing and human cognition into the computing stack, and presents my lab’s work toward this vision. First, I will discuss the co-design of sensing and computation, where we design novel computational image sensors and compile visual programs across heterogeneous sensing and computing hardware. Second, I will discuss co-optimizing computing with humans, where we build novel computational models of human visual perception that provide perceptual, not numerical, specifications and constraints for navigating the enormous design space of visual programs. Together, these projects point toward an exciting future of computing that jointly reasons about machines, the physical world, and human cognition. Bio: Yuhao Zhu is an Associate Professor of Computer Science, Brain and Cognitive Sciences, and an Asaro Biggar Family Fellow in Data Science, all at University of Rochester, where he and his students are mostly drawn to research problems at the intersection of computer architecture, sensing, and human factors. With his collaborators and students, he has won multiple IEEE Micro Top Picks in Computer Architecture for "novelty and potential for long-term impact," along with best paper awards/nominations at MICRO, HPCA, ASPLOS, and IEEE VR. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems
